hints: Think about what must stay exactly the same for two compounds to be called isomers, count the atoms of each element.
Think about what must be different in how those same atoms are joined together, consider connectivity and order.
walkthrough:
Fix what is the same**
Picture two different bottles that both contain exactly $\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}$. Isomers always start from the same stock of atoms. So the first idea is same molecular formula, meaning the same number of $\mathrm{C}$ atoms and the same number of $\mathrm{H}$ atoms.

Pin down what is different**
Now imagine building with those atoms like Lego. You can join them in a different order to make a straight chain in one case and a branched chain in another. The covalent connectivity changes, so they have different structural formulae. That combination is structural isomerism.

Final answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula / same number of atoms of each element.
With different structural formulae / different arrangement of atoms in connectivity.

hints: Compare with structural isomerism and ask what would happen if the order the atoms are joined in stays exactly the same.
Think about the word stereo as meaning in space, and how the same structure could still be arranged differently in three dimensions.
walkthrough:
Keep the connectivity identical**
Here nothing about the bonding order changes. Both isomers have the same molecular formula and the same structural formula, so the same atoms are joined to the same neighbours.

Change only the 3D arrangement**
What differs is how those joined atoms sit in space. Think of cis and trans around a $\mathrm{C=C}$ bond, or mirror images around a chiral carbon. Same connections, different spatial orientation, that is stereoisomerism.

Final answer: Compounds with the same molecular and structural formula.
With different arrangement of atoms in space / different spatial arrangement.

hints: Draw out $\mathrm{CH_2=CH(CH_2)_2CH_3}$ and look closely at the two carbons of the $\mathrm{C=C}$ bond, check what is attached to each one.
Recall the two types of stereoisomerism at AS level and test pent-1-ene for each one, look for a carbon with four different groups.
walkthrough:
Test for geometrical isomerism**
Write pent-1-ene as $\mathrm{CH_2=CHCH_2CH_2CH_3}$. Focus on the double bond. The left carbon, C-1, is bonded to two $\mathrm{H}$ atoms. For cis-trans isomerism each $\mathrm{C=C}$ carbon must carry two different groups. Because C-1 carries two identical $\mathrm{H}$ atoms, swapping them gives no new arrangement, so geometrical isomerism is impossible.

Test for optical isomerism**
Optical isomerism needs a chiral centre, a carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups. Look through the whole chain of pent-1-ene. Every carbon has at least two identical $\mathrm{H}$ atoms or is part of the $\mathrm{C=C}$ with only three groups. With no chiral carbon present, there is no non-superimposable mirror image, so optical isomerism is also impossible.

Final answer: Reason 1: one $\mathrm{C=C}$ carbon has two identical $\mathrm{H}$ atoms attached / two $\mathrm{H}$s on C-1, so no cis-trans / geometrical isomerism.
Reason 2: no chiral carbon / no carbon with four different groups attached, so no optical isomerism.

hints: Look at the repeat unit and identify the two backbone carbons, remember polymerisation converts a $\mathrm{C=C}$ double bond into two $\mathrm{C-C}$ single bonds.
Reverse that change by re-forming the double bond between the two backbone carbons and adding the side groups $\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$ to the correct carbon.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from polymer to monomer**
Addition polymers form when the $\mathrm{C=C}$ of an alkene opens to make two new single bonds to neighbours. To find the monomer, do the reverse. Take the repeat unit $\mathrm{-CH_2-C(CH_3)(CH_2CH_3)-}$ and put the double bond back between those two backbone carbons.

Write the displayed monomer and name it**
That gives $\mathrm{CH_2=C(CH_3)CH_2CH_3}$. In displayed form show $\mathrm{H_2C=}$ on the left, with a double line for $\mathrm{C=C}$, then the right carbon joined to $\mathrm{CH_3}$ above and $\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$ below. Check the formula is $\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}$, a structural isomer of pent-1-ene. For the name, the longest chain through the double bond has 4 carbons with the double bond at C-1 and a methyl branch at C-2, so 2-methylbut-1-ene.

Final answer: Displayed formula: $\mathrm{H_2C=C(CH_3)CH_2CH_3}$ with all bonds shown, $\mathrm{C=C}$ double bond and all $\mathrm{C-H}$ and $\mathrm{C-C}$ bonds displayed.
Name: 2-methylbut-1-ene.

hints: You need a $\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}$ alkene where each carbon of the $\mathrm{C=C}$ carries two different groups, try moving the double bond away from the end of the chain.
Recall how cis and trans differ in the positions of the alkyl groups across the $\mathrm{C=C}$, draw one form clearly with $\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{H}$ placed on the same or opposite sides.
walkthrough:
Choose the isomer that can show geometrical isomerism**
Pent-1-ene cannot do it, but pent-2-ene can. Write $\mathrm{CH_3CH=CHCH_2CH_3}$. Now the left $\mathrm{C=C}$ carbon carries $\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{H}$, and the right $\mathrm{C=C}$ carbon carries $\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{H}$. Each double bond carbon has two different groups and rotation is restricted, so two spatial forms exist.

Draw one form and match the name**
Draw the $\mathrm{C=C}$ horizontally. For the trans (E) form, put the two $\mathrm{H}$ atoms on opposite sides, for example one up and one down, with the carbon chains also opposite. For the cis (Z) form, put them on the same side. Label exactly what you drew: trans-pent-2-ene if opposite, cis-pent-2-ene if same side. The name and the drawing must agree.

Final answer: Structure: displayed or skeletal structure of $\mathrm{CH_3CH=CHCH_2CH_3}$ as one geometrical isomer, e.g. trans with $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups / $\mathrm{H}$ atoms on opposite sides of $\mathrm{C=C}$, or cis with them on the same side.
Name: trans-pent-2-ene (E-pent-2-ene) for the trans structure OR cis-pent-2-ene (Z-pent-2-ene) for the cis structure, name must match structure drawn.
